title: Race Conditions, Deadlocks and Synchronisation Primitives
objectives: Identify race conditions from interleavings of unsynchronised read-modify-write code
Choose between mutexes, spinlocks and atomics based on critical-section length and contention
Compute worst-case wait on a contended lock and Amdahl speedup limits
Analyse a locking scheme for deadlock using the Coffman conditions and global lock ordering
motivation: Two threads each add 30 shares to a position of 100; sometimes the book ends at 130, sometimes 160, and the audit never finds which run was wrong. Races, lock convoys and deadlocks are not theoretical: the order-management system that holds the risk lock during a fast market is the classic quant-dev war story. This lesson makes the failures concrete and countable.

blocks.text: Race conditions: when timing decides correctness

blocks.md: A **race condition** exists when two tasks read-modify-write shared state and the result depends on interleaving. It is not exotic: counter = counter + 1 is three steps, load, add, store, and the scheduler may swap threads between any two of them. The bug hides because most runs interleave benignly; only under production load does the unlucky interleaving appear, and by then it is 4:30 pm before expiry.

blocks.title: Worked example: a lost update
items: counter = 5. Threads A and B each execute counter += 1, unsynchronised.
A loads 5. The scheduler preempts A before it stores.
A resumes with its stale value, adds, stores 6.
Final counter = 6, not 7: B's update was erased, and rerunning the program may give 7, which is why the bug hides.

blocks.caption: Two threads, one million increments each. Run it repeatedly: it prints a different number below 2000000 almost every time, classic lost updates.

blocks.text: Primitives: mutexes, spinlocks and condition variables

blocks.md: Synchronisation primitives make critical sections exclusive. A **mutex** guarantees mutual exclusion: uncontended lock/unlock is a couple of atomic instructions in user space (~20 ns); under contention the kernel puts the loser to sleep via **futex** and wakes it when the lock is released, which costs microseconds. A **spinlock** never sleeps, it burns CPU polling, and only wins when the section is shorter than a couple of switch costs, typically on dedicated cores. **Condition variables** let threads wait for state to change without polling.

blocks.title: Worked example: what a contended lock costs
items: 8 strategy threads share one order-book mutex; the critical section holds it 2 microseconds per update.
The unlucky thread arrives just as the other 7 queue up.
Worst-case wait before its turn even starts: $(8 - 1) \times 2\,\mu s = 14\,\mu s$.
Hold time, not lock count, drives the tail: halve the section and you halve the worst wait. Shard the book (one mutex per instrument) and waits vanish unless instruments collide.

regions.name: heap
regions.note: one order book, one mutex guarding it

blocks.caption: Everything except the two stacks and TLS is shared memory, which is exactly where races live.
Same counter, same two threads, now serialised: exactly 2000000, every run. The lock costs microseconds; the race cost correctness.

blocks.md: A **deadlock** is a cycle of waiting that no schedule can break. Four conditions must all hold (Coffman): **mutual exclusion**, **hold-and-wait**, **no preemption**, and **circular wait**. The practical fix attacks circular wait: impose one global lock order, and every thread acquires locks in that order, so a cycle becomes impossible.

blocks.caption: A fragment, not a program, the comment is the invariant. Any code path that takes risk first can deadlock against this one. Deliberate fragment: surrounding service definitions and initialisation are required.

blocks.md: One more trap: **priority inversion**. A low-priority thread holding a lock blocks a high-priority waiter while medium-priority work preempts the holder, the well-documented 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets are the canonical public incident. The cure is priority inheritance, where the holder temporarily inherits the waiter's priority. For desk systems the moral is simpler: never run the lock-holding housekeeping thread at a lower priority than the threads that wait on it.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amdahl's law caps threading
items: A pipeline is 95% parallelisable; the 5% serial part is one shared-book mutex section. Threads: N = 16.
Total time relative to the serial version: $0.05 + 0.0594 = 0.1094$.
Speedup = $1 / 0.1094 \approx 9.14 \times$, not 16x, the lock-serialised fraction caps everything.

guidedExercise.prompt: counter = 100. Thread X runs `counter += 30` and thread Y runs `counter += 30`, unsynchronised, and the scheduler interleaves them worst-case. (a) Give the final value. (b) If counter is a position in shares, how many shares did the lost update silently drop? (c) Which primitive fixes it, and what does the correct final value become?
hints: Both threads can load the same stale value before either stores.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Both load 100, both store 130: final = 130. (b) One increment of 30 shares was silently dropped, a real position error, not a rounding error. (c) A mutex (or an atomic fetch-and-add) serialises the read-modify-write; the correct final value is 160.

independentExercise.prompt: An order gateway: 4 threads submit orders through one shared mutex held 5 microseconds per order. (a) Compute the worst-case wait for a thread's order under full contention. (b) The desk shards into 4 per-instrument mutexes; state when contention reappears. (c) Spread orders touch two instruments; state the acquisition discipline that keeps deadlock impossible.
hints: Two locks can only cycle if someone takes them in different orders.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $(4 - 1) \times 5\,\mu s = 15\,\mu s$. (b) When orders on the same hot instrument cluster across threads, sharding removes contention only if traffic really separates. (c) Acquire the two instrument locks in one global order (e.g. ascending instrument ID) in every code path; circular wait then cannot form.

commonMistakes: Assuming a line of C++ is atomic, counter += 1 is load, add, store: three separate steps.
Believing a mutex makes the whole program thread-safe, any shared state outside the critical section is still racy.
Using spinlocks with many runnable threads: they burn cores the scheduler could give to real work.
Taking two locks in different orders on different code paths, a textbook circular wait.
Forgetting the wakeup cost: a contended mutex's expense is the futex sleep/wake, not the atomic instruction.
realWorldApplication: Every database, kernel and browser ships with these primitives; lock-order audits and contention profiling are standard production hygiene in any multithreaded codebase.
quantFinanceApplication: Order-management systems are the canonical deadlock scenario (order book + risk + account locks), and the worst-wait formula is exactly how a desk decides to shard a book or replace a mutex with an atomic ring buffer.
summary: Races come from unsynchronised read-modify-write on shared state; interleaving can erase updates intermittently.
Mutexes sleep under contention (futex, microseconds); spinlocks burn CPU and suit only tiny sections on dedicated cores.
Worst-case lock wait is about (N, 1) x hold time; shrink hold times or shard the data.
Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions; one global lock order makes circular wait impossible.
Amdahl's law: serial or lock-serialised fractions cap speedup, 5% serial on 16 threads gives only about 9.1x.

quiz.prompt: Two threads deadlock on mutexes A and B. Which single discipline makes the deadlock impossible no matter what they do afterwards?
options: Always acquire A before B, one global order
Always unlock in reverse acquisition order
quiz.explanation: A cycle needs someone holding B while waiting for A. If every thread acquires in one global order, no thread can hold the later lock while wanting the earlier one, so circular wait cannot form.

quiz.prompt: 8 threads share one mutex whose critical section holds it for 2 microseconds. What is the worst-case wait (in microseconds) for the thread that arrives last, assuming full contention?
quiz.explanation: It waits behind the other 7: $(8 - 1) \times 2 = 14$ microseconds before its turn even starts.

quiz.prompt: This program runs to completion. What exactly does it print?
quiz.explanation: Both loops are serialised by the mutex, so all 2 x 1,000,000 increments land. Remove the lock and the three-step increment interleaves, the total drops below 2000000, varying per run.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about spinlocks vs mutexes are true?
options: A spinlock suits very short critical sections on dedicated cores, where sleeping costs more than spinning
A contended mutex puts the loser to sleep via futex, freeing the CPU for other work
A spinlock is always faster than a mutex
POSIX guarantees mutexes are strictly FIFO-fair
quiz.explanation: Spinlocks win only when the section is shorter than a couple of sleep/wake costs and the core has nothing better to do. Mutexes pay microseconds to sleep/wake but stop burning CPU; POSIX promises no FIFO fairness.

quiz.prompt: A pipeline is 80% parallelisable and runs on 8 threads. Compute the Amdahl speedup to two decimals.
quiz.explanation: $1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1 / 0.3 = 3.33$: the 20% serial part caps the whole system at about 3.3x, so extra threads stop paying quickly.

quiz.prompt: State what a deadlock is, and name the Coffman condition that global lock ordering removes.
quiz.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a cycle of tasks in which each holds a resource the next one needs, so none can proceed. Global lock ordering removes circular wait, breaking one of the four Coffman conditions.
quiz.explanation: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait; a fixed acquisition order makes the cycle impossible.

flashcards.back: Two or more tasks read-modify-write shared state without synchronisation, so the result depends on interleaving, e.g. two threads doing counter += 1 can lose an update entirely.
Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait, all four must hold for deadlock; breaking any one prevents it.

flashcards.front: Worst-case wait on a contended mutex
flashcards.back: $\approx (N - 1) \times t_{\text{hold}}$: 8 threads x 2 microseconds hold means a 14 microsecond worst wait.
Uncontended lock/unlock stays in user space with atomics (~20 ns); only contention traps into the kernel to sleep/wake (microseconds), so design for low contention, not for lock-free everywhere.
